## NGO Website Development in India: Adding Peer-to-Peer Fundraising Pages Without Breaking Receipts, FCRA or Donor Trust

A peer-to-peer fundraising page lets a supporter, such as a runner, a student group or a family marking a birthday, create their own page for your NGO and ask friends to give. On your website, it is a donation page with a second layer on top: a personal story, a target, a progress display and a link that carries the fundraiser's identity through to the payment. The idea is simple. The hard part, which NGO website development in India has to handle carefully, is that every gift still has to land in the NGO's own account, produce a correct 80G receipt in the actual donor's name, respect FCRA rules where foreign money could arrive, and protect the personal data of the fundraiser, the donors and sometimes the beneficiaries.

This guide is for NGO leaders, fundraising and communications managers and anyone briefing a developer. It explains when peer-to-peer pages are worth building, what the pages need, how money and receipts should flow, what the legal and data risks are, how to moderate pages, and how to measure the result. It does not give legal or tax advice; confirm the points that depend on your registrations with your chartered accountant or legal adviser before you build.

### When peer-to-peer pages make sense

Peer-to-peer fundraising works best when your supporters already have personal networks that care about them, even if those networks have never heard of your NGO. A marathon runner raising funds for a cause is asking friends and relatives to support the person as much as the cause. That reach is the point: it brings in donors you could not have reached with your own mailing list.

It suits NGOs that:

- have an existing base of volunteers, alumni, parents, staff or beneficiaries' families who are willing to ask others;
- run events, challenges, anniversaries or seasonal drives that give fundraisers a reason to start a page;
- can respond to fundraisers quickly with support, thanks and updates;
- already have a working [donation page that donors complete](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-page-design-2026), because a peer-to-peer page inherits every weakness of the page it sits on.

It is a poor fit if your main donation flow is unreliable, if you cannot issue receipts promptly, or if nobody on your team has time to support fundraisers. A dozen neglected personal pages can damage trust more than having none.

There is no need to guess at results. We do not quote average amounts raised or conversion rates here, because they vary by cause, season and audience. Start small, learn from your own data, and expand if it works.

### How it differs from crowdfunding

Peer-to-peer fundraising on your own website is not the same as listing a campaign on a crowdfunding platform. The difference is control. On your website, you own the donor relationship, set the rules, receive funds directly and issue receipts in your own name. On a third-party crowdfunding platform, the platform controls the page, the fees and often the donor data. Our comparison of a [donation website versus a crowdfunding platform](/blog/donation-website-vs-crowdfunding) sets out the trade-offs. Peer-to-peer pages on your own site combine some of the social reach of crowdfunding with the control of your own platform, at the cost of having to build and moderate it yourself.

### The anatomy of a fundraiser page

A good peer-to-peer page is a lightweight version of a campaign page, with a few extra elements.

**Header.** The fundraiser's name, photograph (optional, with their consent), the cause and the campaign they are supporting. The NGO's name and logo should be clearly visible so that donors understand who the money goes to.

**Personal story.** A short paragraph written by the fundraiser: why they are doing this and what the cause means to them. Provide a template with prompts, because blank boxes produce empty pages. Limit length to keep pages scannable.

**Target and progress.** A goal amount and a progress bar, tied to confirmed donations only. Do not count pending, failed or refunded payments. If the target is reached, say so and allow the page to keep receiving gifts.

**Donation form.** The same form as the main donation page, with the fundraiser's identifier attached to each gift. Do not build a second payment flow; reuse the tested one.

**Donor list (optional).** Many pages show recent supporters, such as "Priya donated". This is a privacy question: always give donors a choice to hide their name or amount. Never publish contact details.

**Updates.** A place for the fundraiser to post a short update, such as a photo from the event or a thank-you. Updates keep pages alive and encourage repeat sharing.

**Share tools.** Buttons for WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook and copying a link. In India, the WhatsApp share is the most important one. Provide a pre-written message that the fundraiser can edit, and make sure the link previews well, with a sensible title and image, when pasted into a chat.

**Transparency strip.** A compact line stating the NGO's registration and tax-exemption details and linking to the main transparency page. For what that page should hold, see our article on [building a transparency and impact section](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-transparency-impact-reporting-2026).

### The money flow: the rule that cannot bend

The single most important design rule is that **donations must be paid directly into the NGO's own account** through the NGO's payment gateway, never to the individual fundraiser. The fundraiser creates a page and shares a link; they should never collect money in their personal account and forward it. That arrangement creates tax, accounting and trust problems, and in some cases may raise regulatory issues.

Practical implications:

- The payment gateway account belongs to the NGO. Our article on [payment gateway fees and settlements for NGOs](/blog/ngo-payment-gateway-charges-settlements) explains how settlements work and what to watch.
- Each gift is stored with a campaign identifier and a fundraiser identifier, so that finance can tie every rupee to its source.
- Reconciliation must be able to separate gifts by fundraiser and campaign. If you accept UPI directly, see our workflow for [UPI donation reconciliation](/blog/upi-donation-reconciliation-ngo-workflow).
- Fees: decide who bears the payment-processing fee. Whatever you decide, say so on the page. Do not display "100% goes to the cause" unless it is true after fees, and be careful with such claims.

### Receipts and 80G: the donor is the donor

Where your NGO holds a valid 80G approval, the receipt must be issued to the person who actually gave the money, not to the fundraiser who shared the link. This matters because a fundraiser's friends are the donors; each needs their own name, PAN where they want to claim the deduction, and a receipt that matches the gift.

Design implications:

- The donation form on a fundraiser's page must collect the donor's details exactly as the main form does, including the optional 80G toggle.
- Receipts must show the donor's name, not the fundraiser's.
- Fundraisers may want to see "who gave" for thanking purposes, but they should only see what donors have chosen to share. Do not expose PAN, address or contact details to fundraisers.
- If a company or group pays on behalf of several people, the receipt rules can become more complex. Ask your accountant how to handle it and build only what is needed.

Our guides on [80G-compliant donation platforms](/blog/80g-compliant-donation-platform-india), [automated 80G receipts and common errors](/blog/automated-80g-receipts-ngo-errors) and [80G tax exemption for NGOs](/blog/80g-tax-exemption-ngos-compliance) cover the receipt requirements in more detail. If you file annual donation statements, make sure peer-to-peer gifts are included in the data your accountant uses.

### FCRA and foreign donors

Peer-to-peer pages travel. A fundraiser in Pune shares a link with a cousin in Dubai or a college friend in the United States, and a foreign donor appears. If your NGO is not registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, it generally cannot accept foreign contributions. If it is registered, foreign contributions must follow the rules for receiving and using them, including routing through the designated bank account.

This creates design choices:

- **If you cannot accept foreign contributions,** the form should clearly say so, and the payment configuration should decline foreign cards or foreign-currency payments where your gateway supports it. Do not leave this to chance.
- **If you can,** the foreign-contribution path must be separate from the domestic one, with the right account, records and disclosures. Do not let a fundraiser's page route foreign money into a general account.
- **Whichever applies,** decide what happens when an unexpected foreign payment arrives, and write the procedure down before launch.

FCRA is a specialist area and the rules and forms change from time to time. Take advice from someone who handles it professionally, and see our article on [FCRA payment gateway setup](/blog/fcra-payment-gateway-setup-ngos) for the technical side.

### Personal data: three groups of people

A peer-to-peer system involves at least three groups, each with different data protection considerations under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act and its rules.

**Fundraisers.** You collect their name, contact details and often a photograph and a story. Tell them what you will do with it, including that the page will be public. Let them edit or remove their page. Do not use their data for unrelated marketing without a proper basis.

**Donors.** They give name, contact details and sometimes PAN. Tell them how it will be used. Keep marketing consent separate from the donation, and do not pre-tick boxes. A fundraiser must not receive donor contact data without the donor's agreement.

**Beneficiaries.** If a fundraiser's story or your campaign material features children or other vulnerable people, you need consent and strong safeguards. The law has particular rules around children's data, and ethically, photographs of beneficiaries should be used with care. Provide guidance to fundraisers: do not post identifiable photographs of beneficiaries unless the NGO has provided approved material and consent.

Our guide on [donor data protection under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026) lists the practical steps. Because the rules are being phased in, check the current position with a qualified adviser.

### Moderation: protecting the cause and the fundraiser

An open "create your own page" feature invites misuse unless you plan for it. Common risks and responses:

| Risk | Sensible control |
|---|---|
| Fake or fraudulent pages using your name | Require email or phone verification before a page goes live; review pages before they are public, at least at first |
| Inappropriate or false claims in the story | Provide a story template; hold pages for approval until the NGO trusts the process; allow reporting of pages |
| Misuse of beneficiary images | Disallow uploading beneficiary photos; offer an approved image library |
| Fundraisers asking for money outside the site | Instruct on the page and in the welcome message that donations are only accepted through the NGO's page; remove pages that breach this |
| Spam and bots creating pages | Rate limits, verification and a simple bot check |
| Fundraisers who abandon pages | Automatic reminder emails or messages; archive inactive pages after a stated period |
| Offensive content | Moderation queue and a clear acceptable-use policy |

The system needs an admin view where a staff member can see new pages, approve or reject them, edit or remove content and message the fundraiser. If your team is small, build the minimum: a list of pages awaiting approval and a way to unpublish. A fully manual approval queue is usually enough for the first campaigns.

### Setting up the fundraiser's journey

The fundraiser is your user too, and their experience determines whether pages get shared. If the fundraisers are taking part in a walkathon or charity run, see our guide to [building the event registration page](/blog/) for how sign-up, capacity and check-in fit around their pages.

1. **Start.** A clear "Start your own fundraiser" button on the campaign page, not hidden in the menu.
2. **Sign-up.** Ask for name, mobile number or email, and a password or one-time code. Keep it short.
3. **Page builder.** Pre-filled title, suggested target, story prompts and a photograph upload. Offer a preview before publishing. On mobile, make sure it works with a phone camera.
4. **Share kit.** Immediately after publishing, show share buttons and a pre-written WhatsApp message. Provide a downloadable image for status posts, if you have one.
5. **Dashboard.** Let the fundraiser see the total raised, number of donors who consented to be shown, and recent updates. Allow them to post an update and to thank donors.
6. **Messages.** Automated thanks when a gift arrives, a reminder if the page is inactive, and a closing message with a summary. WhatsApp is often the best channel; see our [WhatsApp service](/services/whatsapp-flow) and the guide to [sending donation receipts on WhatsApp](/blog/whatsapp-donation-receipts-ngos).
7. **Close.** A defined end, either at the campaign date or after a period of inactivity, with a message explaining what was raised and what it achieved.

### Campaign tracking and reporting

Peer-to-peer fundraising produces data your team can use, provided it is captured from the start.

Record for every gift: the campaign, the fundraiser, the source (WhatsApp, Instagram, email, direct link), the date, the amount and whether the donor chose a monthly option. Then you can answer questions that matter:

- Which fundraisers brought in the most donors, and which brought in the largest gifts? (These are often different people.)
- Which campaigns produced donors who gave again?
- Which share channel worked best?
- What proportion of fundraisers who created a page received at least one gift?
- How many donors from fundraiser pages gave a second time to the NGO directly?

The last question is the most valuable. A peer-to-peer gift is an introduction; whether it becomes a relationship depends on what happens after. Plan a welcome message for new donors, with their consent, using ideas from our guide to the [donor welcome journey](/blog/ngo-donor-welcome-journey). Our guides on [fundraising dashboard metrics](/blog/ngo-fundraising-dashboard-metrics) and [campaign attribution for fundraising](/blog/ngo-campaign-attribution-fundraising) explain how to put these measures on a dashboard.

### Technical considerations for your developer

If you are briefing a developer or agency, include these requirements:

- **Reuse the existing payment and receipt flow.** A fundraiser page should add an identifier to the existing gift, not create a new payment path.
- **Idempotent payment handling,** so that a payment confirmation received twice does not create two gifts or two receipts.
- **Server-side validation** of target amounts, text length and image size and type.
- **Safe sharing metadata,** including a page title, description and image for link previews, and a clean address that does not expose internal identifiers.
- **Search engine settings.** Decide whether fundraiser pages should be indexed. Many NGOs choose to keep individual pages out of search results to avoid thin, duplicated pages and protect fundraisers' privacy, while the campaign hub page remains indexable.
- **Performance on mobile.** Most visitors arrive from a WhatsApp link on a phone. Our article on [building for donors on slow phones](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-low-bandwidth-mobile-donors-2026) explains what to optimise.
- **Accessibility.** Progress bars, forms and buttons should work with screen readers and keyboards; see our article on [accessibility and donor trust](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-accessibility-donor-trust-2026).
- **Admin controls** for approval, edit, unpublish, refund handling and data export.
- **Backup and logging,** so that a dispute about a gift can be traced.
- **Language support** if your fundraisers and donors prefer Hindi, Marathi or other languages; see our guide to the [multilingual NGO website](/blog/multilingual-ngo-website-india-2026).

### Building it in stages

You do not need every feature at launch. A staged approach reduces risk.

**Stage one: a manual pilot.** Choose a single campaign and invite a small group of trusted fundraisers. Create their pages yourselves using a template on the existing site, with a campaign identifier on each link. This tests whether your supporters will fundraise and gives you real lessons at low cost.

**Stage two: a self-service builder with moderation.** Let fundraisers sign up and create pages that go live after approval. Add the dashboard and automated messages.

**Stage three: scale.** Add team pages (for example, a school with several fundraisers), leaderboards if appropriate for your culture, corporate matching, recurring gifts from fundraisers' pages and integrations with your CRM. See our article on [donor CRM software for Indian NGOs](/blog/ngo-donor-crm-software-india-2026) for the data side.

At each stage, review what happened before deciding what to build next.

### Common mistakes

- **Building before testing demand.** A pilot costs little; a full system nobody uses costs a lot.
- **Letting fundraisers collect money themselves.** Always route funds directly to the NGO.
- **Issuing receipts to the fundraiser.** The receipt must follow the actual donor.
- **Ignoring foreign payments.** A shared link can reach anywhere.
- **Overstating impact.** Progress claims and "your gift will do X" statements must reflect real programme costs and outcomes.
- **No moderation plan.** Decide who approves pages and who responds to problems before launch.
- **No follow-up.** Fundraisers and donors should be thanked, updated and invited to stay involved.
- **Making fundraisers do technical work.** If creating a page takes more than a few minutes on a phone, most will abandon it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a peer-to-peer fundraising page for an NGO?

It is a personal fundraising page that a supporter creates on the NGO's website to ask their own friends and family to donate. Gifts are made through the NGO's normal payment flow, with the fundraiser's identifier attached so the NGO can track and thank them.

### Who gets the 80G receipt on a fundraiser's page?

The donor who made the gift, not the fundraiser who shared the link, provided the NGO has valid 80G approval and the donor's details are captured correctly. Your accountant should confirm how receipts and annual donor statements are to be prepared for these gifts.

### Can a peer-to-peer page accept foreign donations?

Only if the NGO is registered under FCRA and routes foreign contributions through the required account and process. If it is not registered, the form and payment settings should make clear that foreign contributions cannot be accepted. Take specialist advice before enabling any foreign payment path.

### Should fundraiser pages be visible on Google?

Many NGOs keep individual fundraiser pages out of search results, to avoid thin, repetitive pages and to protect fundraisers' privacy, while keeping the main campaign page indexable. Decide this deliberately with your developer, and make sure fundraisers know their page may be publicly viewable by anyone with the link.

### How much does it cost to add peer-to-peer fundraising to an NGO website?

It depends on whether you start with a manual pilot or a self-service system with moderation, dashboards and automated messages. Costs also depend on your existing donation platform. A written quote against a clear requirements list is the only reliable figure, and a small pilot is a sensible first step before committing to a full build.
